definition: In historical psychology, fascination refers to the exercise or experience of a peculiar captivating influence over a person. Older discussions placed it alongside trance, hypnosis, and magical influence.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Charm; pinned source text

reasons: The packet supports an active sense of “to exercise a peculiar or fascinating influence,” but it does not support adding “the experience of” that influence.
“Magical influence” goes beyond the packet, which links the term to the practice of magic rather than defining fascination itself as magical influence.

The packet does not provide a definition of the term “fascination”; it only mentions “so-called FASCINATION, TRANCE, and HYPNOSIS” as contexts where the verb “to exercise a peculiar or fascinating influence” is used.

The definition claims “fascination refers to the exercise or experience of a peculiar captivating influence over a person.” This idea is only implied by the packet’s definition of “Charm” (verb sense 2: “exercise a peculiar or fascinating influence”), but the packet does not explicitly connect that to “fascination” as a term’s meaning.

The definition’s reference to “older discussions placed it alongside trance, hypnosis, and magical influence” is not directly supported as a statement about “fascination” itself; the packet mentions the trio and then discusses magic in the general usage of “charm,” without defining “fascination.”
Therefore, substantive claims about “fascination” and the requested sense of the term are not fully supported by the supplied packet.
